summaryDescription: An apron (Tib. pangden) such as this was worn by all Tibetan women on coming of age at around 16 years old. summaryDescription: This distinctively cut jacket is worn as Nepalese court or official wear, paired with trousers of the same material.  A similar form also occurs with sleeves.  This jacket is made of an unusual glazed cotton fabric, quilted all over and with a larger, geometric quilted pattern forming a border.  The origin of this style of garment is unclear, but is probably to be found in northern India.  Coasts and jackets with side fastenings are widespread in both India and Tibet, Nepal's closest neighbours.  However, a Tibetan garment would normally use a button- and loop-fastening as a closure, while fabric ties like those on this garment are the more common means of fastening in India.

physicalDescription: The figure stands with his legs apart off-centre to the wavy, striped back-slab behind him, upon an inverted lotus base. He has large circular earrings attached to his long ears either side of his tilted head on which he wears a lobed helmet-like hat. He is adorned further with a necklace and armband ( bazubands), together with a long encircling garland. Ends of a pleated scarf are shown flying out on either side, denoting a certain movement in the figure.

physicalDescription: The soap-stone carving is of a well-dressed warrior possibly identified as Arjuna. He is shown standing facing towards his right wielding a sword in his right hand hel against his chest, with his left arm hanging down holding a shield in his left hand. He is wearing a cockaded headdress with looped ribbons at the sides and floral embellishments hanging either side of his head. He is wearing a dhoti down to his knees with a pleated patkatied round his waist which falls to his ankles. He is ornamented with plain anklets over bare feet, armbands, and a kantha (a broad, flat necklace) round his neck. A beaded sacred thread undulates across his chest and an uttariya (scarf) s looped over his shoulders with the long ends flaring out at the bottom either side of him. He is set against a wavy background on a pointed arched backslab with a margin decorated with flame motifs. He stands on the ground below which there is a base of lotus petsls and a central floral motif.

physicalDescription: This group consists of two seated figures, a male and female in courtly dress, on a throne-base. These probably represent donors who have had their image made to celebrate their endowment of a temple or festival. They wear jewellery and are seated in a posture more appropriate to royal rather than lay patrons. The male figure probably wore detachable earrings and a crown, now lost. They sit on a lion-supported platform emblazened with a garuda on the skirt. On the throne, directly above beneath each figure, a yantra (sacred diagram) is engraved.

objectHistory:
Imre Leonard Schwaiger was a well-respected dealer in gems, jewellery and eastern works of art. He was of Hungarian descent and, as a young man, he travelled to India where he became expert in appraising them, later becoming the foremost dealer and agent in such objects.
He built up a list of important clients and was friends with Jacques Cartier, looking after Cartier's interests in Delhi and acting as the company's agent in the purchase of gems, jewellery and objets d'art. Schwaiger was also responsible for introducing Cartier to all of the maharajas and other royals during his visit to India for the Dehi Durbar in 1911.
Imre Schwaiger developed a close working relationship with both the Victoria & Albert Museum and the British Museum, assisting them with a number of acquisitions. He also generously donated a number of valuable objects to both institutions.

Purchased from Imre Schwaiger Esq, 39 Brook Street, Grosvenor Square, W.1. This acquisition information reflects that found in the Museum records (Asia Department registers and/or Central Inventory) as part of a 2023 provenance research project.

physicalDescription: Exorciser's nail or dagger (phur-bu), the hilt of cast and incised brass, inset with imitation turquoises and a balas-ruby: the three-edged blade of iron. The elaborate handle is formed of feather-tipped Dorje resting on the triple crown of the Dharmapala Hayagriva. He has three faces, one mild with 'Buddha curls', one moustached and biting his lips, one demonic with protruding tongue. Each has the third eye and a surmounting figure on the crown, which appears to be that of the great Doctor and Reformer Atisha (d. 1055 AD). The grip is a double Dorje and the socket for the blade is a Makara-head. The blade has three edges. Serpents issue from the Makara's mouth down the side of one side of the blade. The Phur-bu is the Tantric Sorcerer's demon-disperser, either in cases of possession, or to pin demons to earth by suspending it point downwards from the lintel if a doorway.
materialsAndTechniques: Non-meteroic iron; cast and incised brass, inset with imitation turquoises and a balas-ruby (spinel)

physicalDescription: Votive plaque, of grey shale, carved in high relief with the figure of the Dhyani-Buddha Amoghasiddha (Don-Grub). He is seated in dhyana posture with the right hand raised in the Abhaya-mudra, whilst the left rests in the lap holding a patra. Overshadowing him is a seven-hooded serpent, or seven serpents whose bodies are plaited in three-ply behind the Buddha with their tails ending on the rich cloth which covers the throne, upon which the Buddha sits, and upon whose front is the Double-vajra. Beside the throne are two Garudas, the vahan of this Buddha. The name 'Amoghasiddha' is incised on the back of the plaque in sanskrit characters.

physicalDescription: The sculpture shows a male figure seated with a female figure on his lap. The central figure has multiple arms bearing numerous implements. On the proper right, the five visible hands hold a drum (ḍamaru), an arrow, a sword,  an elephant goad, and a conch; on the proper left, the five visible hands hold a skull staff, a noose, a bell, and a skull cup. Additional attributes include a yoga-band (yogapaṭṭa) worn around the knee of the central figure. The female figure makes the gesture of giving (varadamudrā) and a variation of the fear-not or teaching gestures (vitarka or abhayamudrā), formed with the ring finger touching the thumb. Both figures are seated atop their mounts, a bull and a lion. The sculpture is cast in copper alloy and is stylistically dateable to the 18th or 19th century.

objectHistory:
Imre Leonard Schwaiger was a well-respected dealer in gems, jewellery and eastern works of art. He was of Hungarian descent and, as a young man, he travelled to India where he became expert in appraising them, later becoming the foremost dealer and agent in such objects.
He built up a list of important clients and was friends with Jacques Cartier, looking after Cartier's interests in Delhi and acting as the company's agent in the purchase of gems, jewellery and objets d'art. Schwaiger was also responsible for introducing Cartier to all of the maharajas and other royals during his visit to India for the Dehi Durbar in 1911.
Imre Schwaiger developed a close working relationship with both the Victoria & Albert Museum and the British Museum, assisting them with a number of acquisitions. He also generously donated a number of valuable objects to both institutions.

Purchased from Imre Schwaiger Esq, 39 Brook Street, Grosvenor Square, W.1. This acquisition information reflects that found in the Museum records (Asia Department registers and/or Central Inventory) as part of a 2023 provenance research project.

physicalDescription: The principal figure is Samvara (Yi-dam) standing with his sakti in yab-yum against a background of flames. On either side are twelve goddesses in various forms.  In each case there is asingle head, having a third eye when in human form.  The symbols held by the four arms are (right) damaru and kartrika appropriate to a special form of the Dakini Na-ro kha-cho-ma (Sarvabuddha dakini).  In the lower left hand corner is Mahakala as protector of science, blue with one head and third eye dancing on a corpse, his four hands holding sword, trident skull-cup and fruit.  The figure on the lower right hand corner is that of Ganesh, also four armed and holding the axe, rosary, bowl of jewels and radish.

summaryDescription: The ankus is a tool for the handling and training of elephants consisting of a metal hook attached to a short handle. The elephant is trained to respond to pressure applied to the sensitive skin behind the ears in much the same manner as horses by spurs. Elephants have been used during religious ceremonies and processions and as mounts for royalty since antiquity. The ankus is therefore found in armouries and temples all across India, often ornately decorated with gemstones, or engraved with passages of sacred text The ankus is one of the eight auspicious objects known as Astamangala in Hinduism, and is associated with certain other religions of the Indian subcontinent. A goad is also an attribute of many Hindu gods, including Ganesha.

summaryDescription: The yantra may be one of a series of geometric diagrams that are believed to hold magical or mystical powers and are used as a tool to aid meditation. Used in both Hindu and Buddhist religions, each yantra may take a different form to represent a particular deity and they can also be transferred onto an object that can be kept as a charm or an amulet. This yantra, having five concentric triangular grooves encircled by eight lotus petals closely resembles a Kali yantra.
physicalDescription: A charm, carved and polished in rock crystal, of unusual form where the symmetry changes from the base to the top, being rounded square at the bottom, rising through a ring of eight stylised lotus petals to a rounded top that has been engraved with six concentric triangular grooves. At the centre, there is a small, raised "pimple".
materialsAndTechniques: Rock crystal, cut and polished using abrasives and abrasive-charged tools.
creditLine: Gift from The Royal Asiatic Society

physicalDescription: Combined oil-ewer and lamp (sukunda), for temple use. Of brass, cast in several parts by the cire-perdue process. The ewer is shaped to resemble a down-turned lotus resting a hemispherical upturned lotus, thre points of contact being covered with skulls; the body has a trumpet-like foot and neck. Rivetted to the front is the shallow leaf-shaped oil-pan, surmounted by an upright backpiece in high-relief with the standing figure of a four-armed Ganapati with his two shaktis Buddhi and Siddhi standing on either side of him. The elaborate handle is also rivetted on, it is in the form of the seven-headed Naga Sesha who overshadows in his hood the god Vishnu borne upon the shoulders of the Garuda.
creditLine: Bequeathed by the Right Hon. George Nathaniel, Marquess Cuzon of Kedleston.
dimensionsNote: Measurements converted from register.
briefDescription: Ritual lamp (sukunda), cast brass, Nepal, 19th century

physicalDescription: Combined oil-ewer and lamp (sukunda), for temple use. Of brass, cast in several parts by the cire-perdue process. A ewer-like oil-vessel with trumpet-shaped mouth and expanding ring foot: shallow ovoid oil-pan and S-shaped handle. The ewer is ornamented in low relied with close rows of blue-lotus petals and, round the shoulder, with horizontal bands of flower stems. Rising vertically from the oil-pan is a backpiece with the figure of Shiva Mahakala with six arms riding on the shoulders of Ganesha beneath a floral torana. Flanking this torana are two crouching Nandis with canopies on their backs. The elaborate handle is formed of the Seven-Headed Naga-King Sesha whose hoods overshadow Vishnuholding the Conch (or perhaps the Ayudha Purusha Sankha), whilst Bala-Krishna crawls on the plaited bodies of the Naga.
creditLine: Bequeathed by the Right Hon. George Nathaniel, Marquess Cuzon of Kedleston.

physicalDescription: Manuscript, from a set of three palm-leaf pages (IS.81 to B-1972). Each page has three colums of text written in black ink with a binding hole on each side of the central column. One of the pages has a miniature, in the middle of the central column, showing three figures wearing Bodhisattva ornaments; the central figure of the triad is yellow and the ones on either side are pink. The central and left figures have their right hands in karana mudra, while the right figure has its left hand in karana mudra. The background is dark red, and there is a yellow border on each side of the painting.
creditLine: Given by Mrs Wanda Luba.

physicalDescription: Standing 8-armed Avalokitesvara wearing a pointed 5-tiered crown decorated with faces on three sides. Two arms (from right and left) meet with palms together in front of the chest. The topmost right hand holds a ring between the fingers, another arm on the right side extends palm facing outwards to the side. The bottom-most arm makes the gesture of varada (giving blessings). This is echoed on the left side, with the topmost hand holding a lotus flower. Each arm is decorated with armbands and bracelets. The figure also wears a beaded collar and two earrings in the shape of flowers. A long ribbon-like scarf is draped across the shoulders with its ends extending out from the legs. The folds of the dhoti are shown flaring out from the ankles and pleated down the front of the legs. The waist is tied with a bow from which three strings of beads are attached, falling to just above the knees on each side and then attached to the waist again (with an additional string of beads) at the back of the figure. The back hem of the dhoti is decorated with a narrow band of a scrolling pattern.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Susan Brinkworth
briefDescription: Figure, standing 8-armed Avalokitesvara, copper gilt, Nepal, 20th century

physicalDescription: Image of 8-armed Avalokitesvara standing on a circular lotus pedestal. He is wearing an elaborate pointed and tiered crown inlaid with turquoise and coral from which ribbons and pendants extend. The crown is tied behind the head with ribbons. The upper right hand holds prayer beads in a figure of eight shape, the arm below holds a rope noose, another arm is held in front of the chest with the palm facing forwards with the fingers extending upwards in a gesture of abhayamudra (reassurance and protection from fear), the fourth arm is held palm facing forwards with the fingers down in a gesture of varadamudra (giving blessings). The top left arm holds a small book, another holds a trident and another the stem of a lotus flower. The lower left arm holds an image of Amitabha (?) in front of the body. Each arm is decorated with armbands and bracelets and the figure wears a long bead necklace, ribbons and a collar inset with a single turquoise bead. A band decorated with swastikas is draped across the shoulders. Below the knees the hatched decorative border and folds of the dhoti can be seen. Two metal pegs extend from the soles of the feet which fit into the pedestal base.
materialsAndTechniques: Gilt copper inlaid with turquoise and coral
creditLine: Bequeathed by Susan Brinkworth
briefDescription: Figure, standing image of 8-armed Avalokitesvara, gilt copper alloy, Nepal, 20th century

physicalDescription: Image of the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva, seated cross-legged on a circular pedestal decorated with lotus flowers and a pearl border at the front and a Tibetan inscription on the back. The right hand holds a vajra in front of his chest whilst the left hand, resting in his lap, holds a bell. He is wearing armbands, a long necklace of circular beads, a collar decorated with a scrolling pattern and an elaborate tiered crown tied by ribbons at the back of his head to which large circular pendants and ribbons are attached. Ribbon-like elements are draped over his arms and his long dhoti falls in folds around his legs.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Susan Brinkworth
briefDescription: Figure, seated image of Vajrasattva, copper alloy, Nepal, ca 19th century

physicalDescription: Pair of earrings made from copper gilt inlaid with turquoise, mother of pearl, red resin, red gems (including rubies), clear gems and glass. At the top is an arch-shaped piece inlaid with red gems and turquoise with a red gem and a leaf-shaped pendant hanging from each end. An oval pendant is attached to the bottom edge of the arch-shaped piece. The pendant has a mother of pearl at its centre and is surrounded by round red gems and then oval darker red/purple gems. All the gems are set in beaded metal mounts.
creditLine: Given by Suzanne Levi
briefDescription: Pair of earrings, silver gilt and semi-precious stones, Nepal, 19th century.

summaryDescription: A type of container or kala used for offerings by Buddhist Newars in the Kathmandu Valley. The offerings to be carried to a shrine and used in worship included food, red powder, flowers and beer or wine in small containers.
physicalDescription: A container of repousse brass decorated in low relief on the exterior.  With an attached handle and separate tray that forms a lid.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht and acquired by him while living in Nepal during the period 1963-67.

summaryDescription: Yantras are ritual diagrams which are used to evoke and worship Hindu or Buddhist deities or to allow yogic mediatational practices to be carried out. The concept of the yantra is similar to that of the mandala with a square outer perimeter "guarding" a series of inner circles culminating in the innermost circle, the point of final concentration during meditation.
physicalDescription: This square three-dimensional yantra is decorated with superimposed geometrical patterns including squares, triangles and circles, most of which are inscribed with Newari text. At the centre of the yantra is a six-pointed star with a triangle and a circle in its centre. The star is encircled by two tiers of lotus petals., with inscriptions in Newari text. At the centre of the yantra is a six-pointed star with a triangle in its centre.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht and acquired by him whilst living in Nepal from 1963-67.
briefDescription: Yantra, Nepal, 18th-19th century

Rings are found at intervals around the edge of the armlet.

briefDescription: Copper armlet for an image

summaryDescription: The multiple pierced holes and cast rings along the edge of this armlet suggest it was originally sewn either onto a dance costume worn by a priest depicting a deity, or onto a costume adorning a metal image of a deity.
physicalDescription: Cast armlet of bronze in lobed form depicting Vishnu in four armed form riding on Garuda with outstretched wings, encircled by intertwined snakes whose hoods and heads rise above the main figures. Smaller images of deities at either side, to the left proper two dancing figures, a Vishnupada or Vishnu's footprints and a Bhairava. To the right proper a Ganesha, a Bhairava, a yantra and a Vishnu riding on Garuda. The armlet's edge is pierced along almost its entire length and has cast loops at intervals.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht and collected by him in Nepal during the period 1963-67.
briefDescription: Copper armlet for an image

summaryDescription: Bhairava, the fierce form of the Hindu deity Shiva, is one of the most important deities worshipped in the Kathmandu Valley. Several large scale images there in metal and stone reveal the prototypes for this much smaller dance mask.
physicalDescription: A cast copper mask representing Bhairava with staring eyes inlaid with silver and gaping mouth and outstrwetched tongue made in sheet brass. Upper and lower fangs are of silver and upper teeth of shell. Hair at each side of the mouth is of inset black glass and small turquoises, similar decoration of the eyebrows in black glass and small turquoises. A third eye is represented in silver and two small brass earrings are inset with alternate rings of red glass and turquoises. The whole of the face is covered with small round red glass bead inset into round cloisons. Inside the reverse of the mask is a padded cloth fillet tied to the copper mask to cushion the wearer.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht and collected by him in Nepal during the period 1963-67.
briefDescription: Copper dance mask decorated with glass and turquoises, Nepal, 19th century

summaryDescription: Together with its pair, IS.26-2009, this large ear ornament was used to decorate the metal image of a Buddhist or Hindu deity. The profuse use of set stones to cover an area completely was characteristic of  jewellery and ornament production during the 18th and 19th centuries in the Kathmandu Valley of Nepal.
physicalDescription: A square ear ornament of silver and silver gilt decorated with an outer square band of cut turquoises, inner concentric circles are set with lapis lazuli, rock crystal and folied glass made to resemble rubies and sapphires. Central round turquoise. Lacks an ear plug attachment at back. Two silver rings attached at back to one of which is fixed an inter-linked silver chain with small ring at the centre of its length.
materialsAndTechniques: Repousse silver, silver gilt and inset stones
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Bequest of Oppi Untracht and formerly in his private collection.
briefDescription: Silver ear ornament set with semi-precious stones, Nepal, 18th century

summaryDescription: Together with its pair, IS.27-2009, this large ear ornament was used to decorate the metal image of a Buddhist or Hindu deity. The profuse use of set stones to cover an area completely was characteristic of  jewellery and ornament production during the 18th and 19th centuries in the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal.
physicalDescription: A square ear ornament of silver and silver gilt decorated with an outer square band of cut turquoises, Inner concentric circles are set with lapis lazuli, rock crystal and folied glass made to resemble rubies and sapphires. Central clear stone, glass or rock crystal. Tubular ear plug attachment at back.
materialsAndTechniques: Repousse silver, silver gilt and inset stones
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht

briefDescription: Silver ear ornament set with semi-precious stones, Nepal, 18th century

summaryDescription: Ink pots such as this were often attached to a pencase forming a set. Used in the Kathmandu Valley of Nepal they reflect the religion and mythology of the culture that gave rise to them. The form of the ink pot itself is almost identical to the purna kalasha or vase used to contain sacred water while vegetation and crocodile like makara or mythological monsters refer to the life giving powers of water.
physicalDescription: A cast brass ink pot of flattened globular form decorated on one side with an sight armed Ganesha and on the other with a four armed Vishnu riding on Garuda. Two crocodiles support rings at either side which hold brass chains for hannging . A central brass chain secures the lid, all three chains attach to one large ring.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Oppi Untrach Bequest and formerly part of his private collection.
briefDescription: Cast brass ink pot, Nepal, 19th century
production: Kathmandu Valley

summaryDescription: The vegetable cutting knife (Newari: kuyin; Nepali: simha chulesi) is placed on the floor, the hinged blade is swung upward and maintains its position. The user squats at the rear, places the right foot on the lion's rump to steady and secure it, and cuts vegetables by pressing them forward against the blade's sharp inner edge (dhar).
physicalDescription: A vegetable cutting knife (Newari: kuyin; Nepali: simha chulesi) iin the form of a lion cast in brass with attached curving iron cutting blade.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht and acquired by him while living in Nepal during the years 1963-67.
briefDescription: Vegetable cutting knife, Nepal, 20th century

bibliographicReferences.free: Porvoo Museum - Oppi Untracht, Marjatta Parpola, Asko Parpola (eds): Metal Marvels: South Asian Handworks, Porvoo Museum, Finland, 1993, plate 205, page 100

production: Piuthan, West Nepal

summaryDescription: Ink pots such as this were often attached to a pencase forming a set. Used in the Kathmandu Valley of Nepal they reflect the religion and mythology of the culture that gave rise to them. Thie form of the ink pot is based on that of the purna kalasha or vase used to contain sacred water.
physicalDescription: Nepalese ink pots (mashidan) were cast in many forms. This one is a classic type, with a curved base, with lugs on each side of the body and on top of the lid. Two pearl borders encircle the neck of the ink pot.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht and acquired by him while living in Nepal during the period 1963-67.
briefDescription: Brass ink pot, Nepal, 19th century

production: Patan, Nepal

summaryDescription: The Newar craftsman's delight in depicting birds and animals is seen to advantage here in the combined forms of peacocks and lion heads which make up this birdcage hook. The object also demonstrates the high level of casting skills possessed by Newar metalworkers. The handle was used to hang the cage outdoors near a window or when taking the bird for a walk.
physicalDescription: Bird cage handle (kara) for a bird cage (panja) incorporates two peacocks and two lion-headed chimeras. The handle is used to hang the cage outdoors near a window or when taking the bird for a walk.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht and collected by him while living in Nepal during the period 1963-67.
briefDescription: Bird cage handle, Nepal, 18th century

bibliographicReferences.free: Porvoo Museum - Oppi Untracht, Marjatta Parpola, Asko Parpola (eds): Metal Marvels: South Asian Handworks, Porvoo Museum, Finland, 1993, plate 203, page 100

production: Patan, Nepal

summaryDescription: A box used to contain offerings decorated with the figure of Durga Mahishasuramardini, Durga killing the buffallo demon Mahisha, one of the most universally worshipped figures in the Kathmandu Valley. Perhaps the box was associated with her worship as the hinge lies at her foot and hence her figure is seen when the lid is raised to take out its contents at a shrine..
physicalDescription: Offering box is rectangular in shape with concave corners. The cover is decorated with repousse work with a central image of Durga Mahishasuramardini ('the crusher of Mahisha, the buffalo demon'). The box is constructed with the hinge at her foot. When the cover is lifted to make the offering, the image is upright and the lid faces the worshipper. The base of the box has side panels containing animals (eg: elephant and horse) and foliate patterns.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht and acquired by him during the years 1963-67 while living in Nepal.
briefDescription: Copper offering box, Nepal, 19th century

bibliographicReferences.free: Porvoo Museum - Oppi Untracht, Marjatta Parpola, Asko Parpola (eds): Metal Marvels: South Asian Handworks, Porvoo Museum, Finland, 1993, plate 202, page 99

production: Nepal

summaryDescription: Used by Buddhists to carry offerings to a temple or wayside shrine. Inside would be placed food (naivedya), red powder (kaye bhava), liquids such as beer or wine in small containers and flowers. The quantity carried here would be sufficient for one offering.
physicalDescription: Offering container (kala) has a lid and a curved carrying handle. The body of the container is divided into three decorative registers. The lowest register has a diaper pattern, above which is a band of intricately patterned lotus petals. The main register contains an image of the Shakyamuni Buddha seated on a double lotus throne in earth touching pose (bhumisparsamudra) and flanked by two attendants holding fly whisks (chamara). The domed lid has a large knob in the centre and is decorated with a lotus petal design, with bands of both foliate scrolls and a diaper pattern.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collecgtion of Oppi Untracht and acquired by him while living in Nepal during the period 1963-67.
briefDescription: Brass offering container, Nepal, 19th century

bibliographicReferences.free: Porvoo Museum - Oppi Untracht, Marjatta Parpola, Asko Parpola (eds): Metal Marvels: South Asian Handworks, Porvoo Museum, Finland, 1993, plate 198, page 98

production: Patan, Nepal

summaryDescription: Used by Buddhists and Hindus to carry offerings to a temple or wayside shrine. Inside would be placed food (naivedya), red powder (kaye bhava), liquids such as beer or wine in small containers and flowers.
physicalDescription: Offering container (kala) has a lid and a curved carrying handle. The body of the container is divided into three decorative registers. Above a band of lotus petals, the lowest register shows a series of deities, each standing inside an arched niche. The central register shows the 8 Newari Buddhist auspicious symbols, ie: the endless knot (sribatsa), flower (pundarika), banner (dhvaja), yak tail (chamara), 2 fish (matsya), umbrella (chatra), 2 crossed staffs (danda) and the conch (shankha). The domed lid has a large knob in the centre and is decorated with a lotus petal design. A metal chain connects the lid to the carrying handle.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly inn the collection of Oppi Untracht and collected by him while living in Nepal during the period 1963-67.
briefDescription: Brass offering container, Nepal, 19th century

bibliographicReferences.free: Porvoo Museum - Oppi Untracht, Marjatta Parpola, Asko Parpola (eds): Metal Marvels: South Asian Handworks, Porvoo Museum, Finland, 1993, plate 197, page 98

production: Patan, Nepal

summaryDescription: This vessel is an example of the skill of the Newar metalworkers of the Kathmandu Valley who were famous for their lost wax casting in bell metal, copper and brass. The bell metal used here was also employed to cast ritual objects such as bells.
physicalDescription: Beer vessel (thapin) with 12 facets, each one linear chased with a Buddhist symbol. All other plain surfaces are linear chased with floral and other patterns.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht, collected by him while living in Nepal during the period 1963-67..
briefDescription: Metal beer vessel, Nepal, 18th century

production: Patan, Nepal

summaryDescription: Sanctified or blessed water, dispensed from containers such as this, plays a significant role in the religious life of Nepal. It is sprinkled on a person during initiations and at the many ceremonies marking the stages of life.
physicalDescription: Water pot (Newari: nila thala; Nepali: jhari) used to contain and pour holy water. The plain bulbous body stands on a flared base that is decorated with leaf motifs. A long, slender spout extends from the shoulders of the pot. The narrow neck flares into a wide mouth decorated with a band of chevron motifs.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht who acquired it during the period 1963-67 while living in Nepal.
briefDescription: Brass water pot, Nepal, 18th century

summaryDescription: The globular, long necked form of this wine vessel together with its decoration of vertical, repeated geometric ornament suggests the influence of North Indian Mughal art of the 18th century.
physicalDescription: Wine vessel (onti) with a bulbous body resting on a flared base and a long, tapering neck flaring to a wide mouth. The body is a series of vertical panels containing stylised flower motifs. The base is decorated with bands of pearls and leaves. A band of stylised flower motifs encircles the shoulders of the vessel and leaf patterns decorate the neck.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht who acquired it in Nepal during the period 1963-67.

summaryDescription: Used by the wealthier classes of Nepal for containing wine the decoration of repeated diapered floral pattern appears to have been borrowed from neighbouring Indian Islamic culture.
physicalDescription: Wine vessel (onti) with a bulbous body resting on a flared base and a long, tapering neck flaring to a wide mouth. The body is chased with a diapered floral pattern. The base is decorated with bands of pearls and bands of leaf motifs encircle the neck.

physicalDescription: Container for horoscope (jata thala) made from a copper sheet body with a brass sheet cover. Bands of incised decoration including foliate patterns and scrolls with flower/leaves on the lid.

objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht and collected by him during the period 1963-67.

summaryDescription: Offerings of panbira, a mixture of areca nut, lime powder and betel leaf, made at marriages were contained in elaborately decorated boxes such as this.
physicalDescription: The cover of the container represents a lotus in high relief. The sides are intricately worked in repoussage with the ground chisel pierced. The container (guebata) was used to hold areca nuts for the making of panbira, offered during a marriage celebration.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht

summaryDescription: Used by Newar boys in the Kathmandu Valley at their ordination ceremony as monks. Boys become temporary monks for a short period of days or weeks as the Buddhist priesthood has been hereditary since at least the 17th century. During their ordination their heads are shaved, they are dressed in yellow monk's robes and are handed a begging bowl for food donations and a staff with a finial such as this. Stopping before a house door they strike the ground causing the rings on the finial (missing here) to jangle and attract attention from those within.
physicalDescription: A cast brass finial for a boy monk's staff in the form of a circle enclosing a miniature chaitya or stupa. Stylised flame ornament encircles the ring form.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
objectHistory: Formerly in the collection of Oppi Untracht who collected it in Nepal during 1964-66.
briefDescription: Cast brass finial for monk's staff, Nepal, 18th century

bibliographicReferences.free: Page 93, Metal Marvels: South Asian Handworks, Oppi Untracht, Poorvoo, 1993.

summaryDescription: Oil lamps of this type were used in daily ceremonies of worship at shrines in the Kathmandu Valley of Nepal. The main vessel contained the oil for the attached lamp and could be replenished using the attached ladle.
physicalDescription: A cast brass oil lamp with fluted body, its shoulder decorated with skulls. Handle in the form of  a nine headed cobra rearing above the top of the vessel its braided bodies form the handle proper. In front of its heads is a female snake deity  holding an offering in both hands. The projecting lamp pan has a Durga image at its rear flanked by tiny images of Ganesha and Vishnu. An oil dispensing ladle is attached by a chain to the handle.
creditLine: Bequeathed by Oppi Untracht
dimensionsNote: Ladle L. 24.5 cm
objectHistory: Formerly in collection of Oppi Untracht who purchased this in Nepal during the period 1964-66
historicalContext: Ceremonial oil lamp.
briefDescription: Oil lamp of cast brass, Nepal, 18th century

physicalDescription: Standing figure of a Buddhist goddess, possibly a Tara, represented in six-armed form. Of cast copper.
creditLine: Purchased from Ulrich von Schrouder.
historicalContext: This is an exceptionally early Nepalese copper image, showing the sophistication of metal casting in the Licchavi period (6th -8th century).  The saviouress is represented in a rare six-armed form; her attributes include a vajra (thunderbolt sceptre), noose (?), lotus (padma), dagger (?) and a sword.  The sixth hand is held to receive a now missing attribute.  She may represent an early form of Tara transmitted from the Mahayanist tradition of eastern India and not preserved in later iconography.
briefDescription: Figure of a Tara or Buddhist goddess, cast copper, Nepal, Licchavi period, c. 8th century
production: Nepal

galleryLabels.text:
Tara
700–800
Licchavi period
This early copper image of the Buddhist goddess Tara shows the
sophistication of Nepalese metal casting in the Licchavi period.
The Licchavis supported both Hinduism and Buddhism. Here
Tara appears in a rare six-armed form, perhaps an early Indian
version that later disappeared from Nepalese sculpture.
Copper
Nepal
Museum no. IS.9-1989

summaryDescription:
Elaborate crowns of this type are worn by Vajracaryas, Buddhist priests when officiating at religious ceremonies in Nepal. Vajracarya, "master of the thunderbolt", is both a caste and family name indicating those entitled to perform priestly functions. They command the highest rank in the Buddhist community, the equivalent of Brahmins in the Hindu context. They typically use both a vajra (thunderbolt sceptre) and ghanta (ritual bell) in these rituals. A painted Nepalese manuscript cover dated 1532 depicts such a crowned Vajracarya engaged in ritual on behalf of a donor and his family at a temple stupa; he is depicted holding both vajra and ghanta and seated before a fire altar and assorted ritual utensils, including an offering dish, mirror and miniature chaityas (stupas). The ritual crown depicted bears close comparison to the V&A example, with its forehead diadem and elaborate superstructure, and the ear-like pendants. 

This crown has individually cast medallions depicting Bodhisattvas positioned around the dome, with Vairocana in the centre; each is framed within an elaborate foliate medallion. The crown is surmounted by a five-pronged half-vajra. A dated inscription (Nepal Samvat 797) invokes Vajrasattva, the supreme deity of the vajra sect. A number of these crowns have survived, but this example is the finest and most complete.
physicalDescription: Ritual crown of gilt copper, set with imitation stones in rock crystal and glass, with applied ornaments including cast and gilt Buddhist figures framed by elaborate scrolling patterns.
materialsAndTechniques: Copper, gilt and cast; set with imitation stones of rock crystal and glass
creditLine: Given by Lt. Col. E.W.A. Armstrong.

1. Ritual Crown
Dated 1677
Malla period
This crown would have been worn by a hereditary Vajracharya
priest of the Kathmandu Valley. The Vajracharyas were originally
celibate Buddhist monks. By the early 15th century they had
been brought within the prevailing Hindu caste structure of
valley society, with a position as one of the highest castes.
Gilded copper set with imitation stones in rock crystal and glass
Nepal
Given by Lt Col. E.W.A. Armstrong
Museum no. IS.5-1946

physicalDescription: Buddhist triptych shrine, with metal hinges. Of wood, carved with figures of divinities etc. In the centre is a trefoil niche, which is empty, flanked by two columns and overhung by a canopy of complicated floral ornament; beside the outer parts of the column stand two figures. Above the canopy is a Garuda, and over him, a seated Buddha. Most of the shrine is carved with figures of divinities within square compartments; some of them are enclosed by spiral stems.
materialsAndTechniques: Wood, carved, with paint and gilding
creditLine: Given by Mrs Preston
historicalContext: The central niche of this triptych, now empty, would have housed an image, either placed directly in the niche or possibly contained within a gau (amulet box), the latter more suitable for transporting.  The niche is flanked by columns with "vase of plenty" (purnakalasa) bases, a feature of Nepalese wooden architecture.  Two attendant deities pay homage and above a particularly  flamboyant torana with garuda, nagas and makaras frame the niche.  This group is surmounted by an image of Amitabha, seated in meditation on stylized rocks.  Numerous deities and guardians occupy the subsidiary niches.  A monk, presumably associated with the commissioning of this shrine, is seen on the lower register.
briefDescription: Portable shrine, carved wood with paint and gilding, Nepal, c.15th-16th century

Portable Shrine
1500–1600
Malla period
The central niche, now empty, would have probably housed a
metal image. The niche surround (torana), with its mythical
animals and two flanking columns, is a miniature version
of door surrounds found in Nepalese wooden architecture.
Below the niche and inside the folding doors are many deities,
including the Twenty-One Taras, an important group of
protective goddesses.
Wood with paint and gilding
Nepal
Museum no. IM.1-1938

summaryDescription: This figure represents the Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, the Buddhist Lord of Compassion. He is seen here in his popular manifestation as Padmapani, the Lotus-holder. Padmapani is a Bodhisattva, an enlightened being who voluntarily postponed passing into nirvana so that he could help others to gain salvation. The concept of the Bodhisattva was developed in the Mahayanist school of Buddhist thought, and gained enormous popularity in the Himalayas and the greater Asian world. The stillness and serenity of this figure speaks of the state of harmony to which the Bodhisattva aspires, whilst the flexed and sensuous pose in which he stands links him to the human world. The Bodhisattva's right hand is lowered in the gesture of granting wishes (varadamudra), and his left hand is poised to support the stem of a lotus (padma), but this is now missing. The figure is richly adorned with jewellery that is inset with precious and semi-precious stones. A five-pointed diadem surrounds his elaborately dressed and raised hair (jatamukuta), which is surmounted by a small image of the Buddha Amitabha of whom Avalokitesvara Padmapani is seen as an emanation. Nepalese Newar craftsmen made this finely jewelled image for Tibetan patrons. The long tradition of Newar craftsmen from the Kathmandu Valley working for Tibetan patrons can be dated back to the 7th century A.D. In 1922 the Victoria and Albert Museum purchased this sculpture from Major Lewis Bathe Rawling (1871-1940). He was the brother of Brigadier-General Cecil Godfrey Rawling (1870 - 1917) who had been a member of the British campaign led by Major Francis Younghusband (1863-1942) which fought its way from India to Lhasa, the capital of Tibet, in 1904. The aim of this military assault was to force Tibet to engage in trade with British India and to counter perceived Russian influence in the region. The Tibetan army proved no match for the British-led forces and thousands were killed. Many objects were brought back to Britain in consequence of the invasion. Some had been purchased, but many had been looted from Tibetan monasteries, temples, and homes. The V&A's archive file of 1922 states that the sculpture was 'Acquired in the Shigatse district, Tibet, in 1904, by the late Brig.-General Rawling'. It has often been assumed that Rawling got the figure during the Younghusband Mission, as it was known, but the invading force did not go to Shigatse. Rawling was, however, one of four officers who made a subsequent journey through Shigatse in September 1904 to survey the site of a new British trade agency at Gartok in western Tibet. The sculpture was either sold or given to Rawling at this time or may even have been part of a diplomatic exchange. One of Rawling’s companions, William Frederick O’Connor (1870-1943), was conducting a covert assignment to form an alliance with the Panchen Lama, Thubten Choekyi Nyima (1883-1937), head of the Tashi Lhunpo monastery in Shigatse, to thwart the influence of the Dalai Lama, Ngawang Lobsang Thubten Gyatso (1876-1933).

The concept of the bodhisattva was developed in the Mahayanist school of Buddhist thought, and it gained enormous popularity in the Himalayas. The stillness and serenity of this figure conveys to the viewer the state of harmony to which the bodhisattva aspires, whilst the flexed and sensuous pose in which he stands links him to the human world.

objectHistory:
Imre Leonard Schwaiger was a well-respected dealer in gems, jewellery and eastern works of art. He was of Hungarian descent and, as a young man, he travelled to India where he became expert in appraising them, later becoming the foremost dealer and agent in such objects.
He built up a list of important clients and was friends with Jacques Cartier, looking after Cartier's interests in Delhi and acting as the company's agent in the purchase of gems, jewellery and objets d'art. Schwaiger was also responsible for introducing Cartier to all of the maharajas and other royals during his visit to India for the Dehi Durbar in 1911.
Imre Schwaiger developed a close working relationship with both the Victoria & Albert Museum and the British Museum, assisting them with a number of acquisitions. He also generously donated a number of valuable objects to both institutions.

Purchased from the dealer Imre Schwaiger, Esq., 39, Brook Street, Grosvenor Square, W. This acquisition information reflects that found in the Museum records (Asia Department registers and/or Central Inventory) as part of a 2023 provenance research project.

historicalContext: Bhairava is a wrathful and vengeful aspect of Siva.  The image is adorned with skulls, snakes form his earrings and necklace and his hair rises in a flame like nimbu.  This is a large scale image, richly decorated with inlaid stones intended for public worship; it has a small opening at the mouth through which blessed liquids were poured for the benefit of devotees.  The cult of Bhairava worship is widely practised in Nepal.  Once a year, to mark the indra-jatra festival, a major image of the Bhairava in the Hanuman Dhoka, Kathmandu, is exposed for public worship.

summaryDescription: This amulet box or ‘jantar’ is of a type made and used by Newars in the Kathmandu Valley of Nepal. Like Tibetan amulet cases, jantars were used to contain prayers written on paper or other blessed objects believed to protect the wearer. This box features the ‘jarao’ inlay technique, which combines the setting of stones in cloisons with filigree wire decoration to cover the surfaces of jewellery and ritual objects. The technique was especially popular during the 18th and 19th centuries. The central face of this example is a mythical Chepu or monster mask.

summaryDescription: During the daily puja or worship of deities in Nepal red powder is placed on the foreheads of the image. The use of a Buddhist stupa or chaitya shaped vessel to contain this reflects the great importance of this central symbol of the Buddha's spiritual achievement for all Buddhists.
physicalDescription: This container in the form of a stupa (Newari: shinomu; Nepali: cholamu) was used for holding vermilion pigment powder. The circular bell-shaped base of the container is decorated with bands of pearl motifs and lotus leaves. The neck is also decorated with bands of small and large pearl motifs on top of which is a shallow cup-shaped container, the rim of which is decorated with a pearl border. On top of the lid is an umbrella of discs in diminishing diameters, suggesting the umbrella form found on top of ancient stupas and symbolising the five elements (earth, water, fire, air and ether).

historicalContext: Indra was the supreme Vedic god of early India, the bearer of the thunderbolt (vajra), associated with rain.  In later Hinduism he retained his role as King of the Gods but ceased to command popular following as a cult  deity.  In Nepal however, he continued to be worshipped by both Hindus and Buddhists as the master of the atmosphere, celebrated in the annual eight day festival of Indra-jatra. He is represented as a king, crowned and bejewelled, seated in royal ease (maharajalila), and identified by his horizontal third eye and the vajra, seen here supported on a lotus.

summaryDescription:
This small copper image shows the Hindu goddess Durga slaying the Buffalo demon Mahisa. Durga is the embodiment of female energy. This power was the only force strong enough to destroy Mahisa, who threatened world order and the authority of the other gods.

The sculpture is an extraordinary example of early Nepalese repousse skills. In this technique the metalworker works from the back or underside of the metal to create the image in relief.

This representation of Durga should have four arms (one is missing here). The four-armed form is rarely seen in Nepal beyond the 11th century, when she typically appears with eight or more arms. The energy of the goddess trampling the buffalo is awesome. Her raised foot would have rested on a lion of the type represented by the ivory throne legs on display in the V&A (Museum nos. IS 269 & A-1960).

historicalContext: Tara, the female aspect of the god of compassion, Avalokitesvara, seen with both hands in the gesture of disposition and reasoning (vitarkamudra), the lower hand also holding the stem of a lotus (padma), her principal attribute.  The tara is wearing a detachable crown of gilt copper with hanging leaves and inlaid silver ribbon, and is seen against an elaborate backplate (prabha) decorated with buddhas and taras supported on lotus thrones (padmapitha), with a pearl and flame border.  The base is decorated with the triratna, the symbol of the "three jewels" of Buddhism: the Buddha, the law (dharma) and the community of monks (sangha).  Figures of this scale were often positioned flanking a temple doorway in a royal or private enclosure.

physicalDescription: This sculpture depicts Uma-Mahesvara, also referred to as Parvati and Shiva. They are both seen here seated in the relaxed lalitasana posture on top of a cushion-throne, over which a tiger skin has been draped. Shiva holds Parvati's waist with his lower left hand, whilst his two right hands are poised in the gesture of vitarkamudra,which signifies teaching or intellectual discussion. His fourth hand would have originally held a trisula or trident, this is now however missing. Amongst Shiva's iconographic attributes are the crescent moon and human skull, these are set on either side of his headdress within the folds of his uncut matted hair. Alongside Shiva sits Nandi, who is his bull vahana or vehicle.
materialsAndTechniques: Copper with gilding and precious stone inlay

900–1000
Late Licchavi/Transitional period
The Hindu deity Shiva with his consort Parvati and the bull
Nandi are seated on a cushion-throne draped with a tiger skin.
This subject was the most popular of all the Hindu themes in
Nepalese sculpture. The earliest surviving examples date from
around the 6th century AD.
Copper with gilding and precious stone inlay
Nepal (Kathmandu Valley)
Museum no. IS.54-1985

physicalDescription: Tangka, a Mandala of Chakrasamvara; gouache on cotton. It features the black form of the deity with a red consort in the central circle of the mandala. The central circle is surrounded by four layers of outward-facing lotus petals. Subsidiary two-armed representations of Chakrasamvara appear in eight radiating lines, including red, white, green, and yellow forms each guarding a gate. Outside the circle of flames guarding the inner area are found representations of 'The Eight Cemeteries', each with its yogi, corpses, wild animals and deity. The inner mandala lies within a painted double rectangular frame of red (inner) and yellow (outer) colour on which are dispersed white skulls and heads respectively. In the spaces between the inner mandala and the painted borders are ten deities, five above anf five below. On the outside of the painted borders is a dense lotus scrollwork inhabited by mythical animals and birds, including peacocks, makara and naga. At either side, dragons and mangooses emit flames.

titles.title: Torana with Garuda attacking a Naga and a Nagini

summaryDescription: This relief would have formed a decorative panel (torana) above an entrance to a temple or above a large metal image of a deity itself. The Garuda, half man and half eagle, is a favourite subject in Nepalese art, and is traditionally represented engaged in mortal combat with its natural enemies, the water spirits or nagas.  The group with its flamboyant open scroll work shows the skill of the Newari metal workers of the Kathmandu Valley at their best.
physicalDescription:
TORANA WITH GARUDA ATTACKING A NAGA AND NAGINI: These reliefs would have been found in the central motif to a decorative panel (torana) above an entrance to a temple or above a large metal image itself.
The Torana (overpiece) is in thrre parts.  The central figure of a flying Garuda, who holds in his claws the leg of a floating Naga and Nagini.  The lateer are overshadowed by three-headed Cobras: they have each four arms.  With one hand each grasps a leg of the Garuda, with two hands they hold jewel-symbols and with the fourth they make  the Abhays mudra before the breast.  Around them is rich foliate ornaments partly in openwork.
materialsAndTechniques: Repoussé copper, with gilding and paint, set with turquoise, rock crystal and semi-precious stones

TORANA WITH GARUDA ATTACKING A NAGA AND NAGINI: These reliefs would have found the central motif to a decorative panel (torana) above an entrance to a temple or private enclosure. The Garuda is a favourite subject in Nepalese art, and is traditionally represented engaged in mortal combat with his natural enemies, the nagas. The Garuda's claws can be seen gripping the naga and his companion, the Nagini. The group with its flamboyant open scroll work shows Newari metal figure working skills at its best.

summaryDescription: Lion throne supports such as these were found in India from at least the 1st century AD as shown on early sculptural relief. Ivory was widely used in India, from the earliest periods, for luxury furniture.
physicalDescription: This pair of lions formed part of a set of throne supports. Ivory was widely used in India, from the earliest periods, for luxury furniture. A third lion in the British Museum bears a label stating that it came from the Jangkor Yangsi monastery, which is situated on the north branch of the Brahmaputra River. Inscriptions on each lion are in a proto-Bengali script probably no later than the 12th century, and support Nepal as the most probable source of these sculptures.
objectHistory: The museum register for the 1960 acquisition of this pair of lions states that 'according to a note by D. Barrett [of the British Museum] the V.&.A. lions were brought from Tibet in 1904 by Maj. A. Wallace Dunlop of the 23rd Sikh Pioneers, who went to Llasa with Younghusband.'  The British campaign led by Major Francis Younghusband (1863-1942) fought its way from India to Lhasa, with the aim of forcing Tibet to engage in trade with British India and to counter perceived Russian influence in the region. The Tibetan army proved no match for the British-led forces and thousands were killed. Many objects were brought back to Britain in consequence of this invasion. Some had been purchased, but many had been looted from Tibetan monasteries, temples, and homes.
briefDescription: Pair of throne legs, ivory, Nepal, 12th century

summaryDescription: This earring is of the type made by Newar craftsmen and used to adorn religious images in the Kathmandu Valley or Tibet. Newars, the indigenous community of the Kathmandu Valley, were well known for their skill as jewellers and for this type of stone encrustation, called ‘jarao work’. The top roundel contains the auspicious and protective monster mask, the lower plaque the peacock, a favourite Newar emblem believed to offer protection against death by snakebite.

summaryDescription: This is a ceremonial necklace ornament or ‘tayo’, used by Newar women of the Kathmandu Valley on important ritual occasions, including marriage. In early forms of these ornaments, the tubular body is hollow, suggesting that they may have been amulet containers, but present examples are entirely closed and so cannot now be used for that purpose. The  Indian origins of this type of ornament are indicated by the teardrop ornament on the upper edge of this example, a motif found on Indian jewellery.

Temple lamp made of rock crystal, carved and incised, with foot and mounts of gilt copper, repousse, inset with 48 cabochon and 16 table white topazes backed with plain or tinted tinsel. Made by a Newari craftsman in Kathmandu.

The gana, like the grotesque in medieval European art, provided the artist with a rare opportunity for caricature and whimsical invention.

objectHistory:
This was part of a collection of Indian, Nepalese, and Tibetan art objects that was purchased in 1913 from Imre Leonard Schwaiger was a well-respected London and Delhi-based dealer in gems, jewellery and eastern works of art. He was of Hungarian descent and, as a young man, he travelled to India where he became expert in appraising them, later becoming the foremost dealer and agent in such objects.
He built up a list of important clients and was friends with Jacques Cartier, looking after Cartier's interests in Delhi and acting as the company's agent in the purchase of gems, jewellery and objets d'art. Schwaiger was also responsible for introducing Cartier to all of the maharajas and other royals during his visit to India for the Dehi Durbar in 1911.
Imre Schwaiger developed a close working relationship with both the Victoria & Albert Museum and the British Museum, assisting them with a number of acquisitions. He also generously donated a number of valuable objects to both institutions.

Purchased from the dealer Imre Schwaiger, Esq., 39, Brook Street, Grosvenor Square, W. This acquisition information reflects that found in the Museum records (Asia Department registers and/or Central Inventory) as part of a 2023 provenance research project.

historicalContext: This embroidery, decorated with scenes from the Hindu epic, the Ramayana, is a rare survivor of textile art from Nepal.  It probably served as a frontispiece to an image shrine or altar, or may have hung along the edge of a canopy.  The subject, one of the most popular in Hindu mythology, is the battle in which Rama defeats the ten-headed demon king Ravanna.  It is illustrated in a continuous narrative.   Aband of garuda and lion masks fill the upper border and masks alternating with coloured banners appear below.  The style of the figures bears close comparison to those in paintings of the Bhaktapur school, to which this embroidery appears to be closely related.

Depicting Vajradhara (‘The Indestructible or Steadfast holder’), a prototype of Vajrapani, seated on a lotus throne. Two-armed, he holds a thunderbolt (dorje) in his right hand and a bell (drilbu) in his left.

objectHistory:
The museum bought this object from the dealers, Messrs Spink and Son.  The archive file notes that it was 'acquired during the British Mission to Lhasa in 1904'. This military campaign led by Major Francis Younghusband (1863-1942) fought its way from India to Lhasa, with the aim of forcing Tibet to engage in trade with British India and to counter perceived Russian influence in the region. The Tibetan army proved no match for the British-led troops and thousands were killed. Many objects were brought back to Britain in consequence of the invasion. Some had been purchased, but many had been looted from Tibetan monasteries, temples, and homes.  The object is attributed in the file to 'Shigatse Monastery', presumably Tashi Lhunpo. However, the invading force did not go to Shigatse, so it may have been acquired during a subsequent mission in the region.

objectHistory: Provenance: Purchased from Imre Schwaiger in 1910, a well-known art dealer of Hungarian descent, with offices in London and colonial India (Delhi, Bombay, Calcutta, and Simla). This acquisition was part of a collection of Indian and Tibetan objects purchased by the V&A from Schwaiger in 1910 for £1000. A total of forty-nine objects produced or acquired in Tibet were procured from Schwaiger between 1910 and 1919, but it remains challenging to determine when, where and how they were acquired. In the V&A archives, we have some indication that some of the Tibetan objects from Schwaiger may have been looted or otherwise acquired in Tibet during the British military assault led by Colonel Francis Younghusband in 1903-04. However, recent scholarship by Dr Emma Martin (Past & Present, 2025) also establishes that Schwaiger acquired Tibetan objects in colonial India. He had cultivated close ties with the British colonial administration in India and was approached to appraise and acquire Tibetan objects from the 'Toshakhana', a British-instituted treasury that collected and processed diplomatic gifts. Some of the Tibetan objects collected by Schwaiger in India may have been diplomatic gifts from Tibet and its representatives, such as those sent by the thirteenth Dalai Lama, Thubten Gyatso, to the Viceroy of India, Charles Hardinge, and other British representatives during the Shimla Convention negotiations in 1913-14. According to Martin, the toshkhana also sold off diplomatic gifts received by colonial officers and agents based at British trading stations inside Tibet at Yatung, Gyantse, and Gartok. The acquisition information for this object has been updated following provenance research conducted during the AHRC-funded 'Reanimating Tibetan Heritage' project (2024-2026).

summaryDescription: Miniature architecture is part of the religion and rituals of many different cultures. This hanging oil lamp was made for use in a Hindu temple. Its shape closely follows that of the Krishna temple built in 1637 in Patan, Nepal. The four oil trays, pendants, chain and the small birds and animals on the side are additions. Architectural motifs often appear on ritual objects such as incense burners, lamps and shrines.

summaryDescription:
This image shows a female donor seated in royal ease with her hands raised in ‘anjali’, in reverence of her god. The woman is dressed in richly detailed textiles and wears an array of fine jewellery. The luxurious clothes and adornments suggest that she is a person of high rank, possibly a member of the ruling Malla household of the Kathmandu valley. 

This figure was originally riveted to a pedestal. We may presume that she formed part of an ensemble, together with her husband, revering an image of the deity they have donated. 

The figure is made from sheet copper which has then been mercury gilded. This was a widely used medium in the later Malla period (about 1200-1768) and permitted the creation of larger-scale devotional images than solid cast copper would allow.

There is a long tradition of acknowledging the role of donors as patrons of Indian religious art. It initially took the form of donor inscriptions that recorded their philanthropy and meritorious intentions. Later, donor portraits appeared. Such portraits have been part of Nepalese art since the Licchavi period (about 300-800 AD). There are, for example, donor portraits at the great Vaisnava temple of Changu Narayan, where the earliest sculptures span the period from 600-800 AD.

objectHistory:
This was part of a collection of Indian, Nepalese, and Tibetan art objects that was purchased in 1913 from Imre Leonard Schwaiger was a well-respected London and Delhi-based dealer in gems, jewellery and eastern works of art. He was of Hungarian descent and, as a young man, he travelled to India where he became expert in appraising them, later becoming the foremost dealer and agent in such objects.
He built up a list of important clients and was friends with Jacques Cartier, looking after Cartier's interests in Delhi and acting as the company's agent in the purchase of gems, jewellery and objets d'art. Schwaiger was also responsible for introducing Cartier to all of the maharajas and other royals during his visit to India for the Dehi Durbar in 1911.
Imre Schwaiger developed a close working relationship with both the Victoria & Albert Museum and the British Museum, assisting them with a number of acquisitions. He also generously donated a number of valuable objects to both institutions.

Purchased from the dealer Imre Schwaiger, Esq., 39, Brook Street, Grosvenor Square, W. This acquisition information reflects that found in the Museum records (Asia Department registers and/or Central Inventory) as part of a 2023 provenance research project.

summaryDescription: These earrings are of the type made by Newar craftsmen and used to adorn religious images in the Kathmandu Valley or Tibet. Newars, the indigenous community of the Kathmandu Valley, were well known for their skill as jewellers. The fronts of the earrings are decorated with ‘jarao work’, which uses metal cloisons filled with stones and additional filigree wire. This was popular amongst Newar metalworkers during the 18th and 19th centuries. In this example, a silver and silver-gilt plate is encrusted with turquoise, lapis lazuli, coral, pearl, feldspar, zircon, pink and blue sapphire, aquamarine, emerald and diamond.

summaryDescription: This ceremonial necklace or ‘suta’ is of the type worn during initiation ceremonies by Newar boys and girls in the Kathmandu Valley. The same type of necklace is also placed as decoration around the necks of religious images. The use of carved coral at the centre of a piece of jewellery, as in this example, is a typical feature of Newar jewellery. Here the coral is carved in the form of the Hindu god Ganesh, with two flanking rubies held by dragons.

summaryDescription: This type of ceremonial necklace, called ‘tikma’, is worn by Newar women of the Kathmandu Valley at many life-cycle ceremonies, including girls’ initiation ceremonies. It is also worn at marriages and by dancers portraying female deities. The pale inset turquoises are carved with representations of the Hindu god Vishnu, who rides his vehicle Garuda. In a culture in which Hindu and Buddhist iconography and worship practices have in many cases blended, this iconographic programme would not prevent its use by a Buddhist family.

summaryDescription: This silver-gilt forehead plaque is covered with turquoise, coral, lapis lazuli, rubies, sapphires, diamonds, aquamarine, zircon and freshwater pearls. Such forehead ornaments were fitted to large religious images by means of the hooks at each end. The Buddha figures represented in this example - at the centre, the red Amitabha Buddha, flanked by images of blue Buddha Akshobhya - suggest that it may have adorned a crowned image of one of the Five Meditational Buddhas, symbolic embodiments of particular aspects of Buddhahood. Images decorated with forehead plaques may still be seen in some shrines of the Kathmandu Valley today.

objectHistory:
This was part of a collection of Indian, Nepalese, and Tibetan art objects that was purchased in 1913 from Imre Leonard Schwaiger was a well-respected London and Delhi-based dealer in gems, jewellery and eastern works of art. He was of Hungarian descent and, as a young man, he travelled to India where he became expert in appraising them, later becoming the foremost dealer and agent in such objects.
He built up a list of important clients and was friends with Jacques Cartier, looking after Cartier's interests in Delhi and acting as the company's agent in the purchase of gems, jewellery and objets d'art. Schwaiger was also responsible for introducing Cartier to all of the maharajas and other royals during his visit to India for the Dehi Durbar in 1911.
Imre Schwaiger developed a close working relationship with both the Victoria & Albert Museum and the British Museum, assisting them with a number of acquisitions. He also generously donated a number of valuable objects to both institutions.

Purchased from the dealer Imre Schwaiger, Esq., 39, Brook Street, Grosvenor Square, W. This acquisition information reflects that found in the Museum records (Asia Department registers and/or Central Inventory) as part of a 2023 provenance research project.

summaryDescription: This unusual jacket is based on European military styles or riding habits, although obviously intended for quite a small Nepalese woman.  The materials used are also far from the usual military conventions, combining European patterned velvets with elaborate cuffs, epaulettes and front panels heavily embroidered with seed pearls, sequins and gold-wrapped thread.  Western dress uniforms contributed a great deal to formal wear in northern India and Nepal during the later nineteenth century, with many hybrid garments coming into vogue at the Indian and Nepalese courts.  This little jacket is an example of just such a garment, looking more like a piece of theatrical costume than something worn by a young courtier in Kathmandu in the 1850s.

physicalDescription: Vajracharya crown, of hammered and gilt copper, with applied ornaments of cast and chased brass inset with pieces of turquoise and imitation gems of glass backed with coloured foil. The crown is in the form of a three-tiered cone with a finial composed of an open lotus upon whose seed-capsule sits the Adi-Buddha in his form of Vajrasattva beneath a four-pronged Thunderbold (Vajra). Across the brow of the crown are five cast and chased 'leaves' of openwork brass, each with a seated figure of one of the Five Buddhas of the Vajradhatu mandala, Vairochana occupying the centre with Amitabha, Amoghasiddhi, Akshobhya, and Ratnasambhava arranged around him. Below these plaques is a fillet mounted with floral forms in stones, flanked by fan-like bows and fluttering ends. On the baclk edge of the lowest tier of the cone, are three floriate panels with the seated Green Tara; on the second tier are further plaques with figures of Akshobhya, Amitayus, Avalokita, and a six-armed form of Tara; and on the uppermost tier are four flame-panels. This crown would be worn in Tantric Buddhist rituals.

historicalContext: The goddess Tara was widely worshipped in Nepal and Tibet. The cult was stimulated by Atisa, the Indian teacher who played a major role in stimulating Buddhism in Tibet in the 11th century. Sitatara, the white Tara, has the lotus (padma) attribute and makes the gesture of preaching (vyakhyanamudra) with her raised hand, the other held in varadamudra, the gesture of the granting of wishes. A third eye is indicated on her forehead. This is a mild form of Tara, seen as the female manifestation of Avalokitesvara. Prayers written in Tibetan were found inside the image, indicating that it had been venerated by Tibetans.

physicalDescription: This scroll painting shows a form of Avalokiteshvara.  The fresh and vigorous execution is emphasised by the gilt niche surrounding the central figure.
historicalContext: Amoghapasa, ("He of the Infallible Noose") is a form of Avalokitesvara, the supreme bodhisattva of compassion.  He is invoked as a saviour against natural disaster and physical torment.  Amoghapasa is seen in his eight-armed form (his most distinctive attributes being the trident (trisula) and noose (pasa), being worshipped by the goddess Brkuti to his left and by the green Tara to his right.  Lesser deities pay homage below and emanations appear above.  The bodhisattva is enthroned on a magnificent platform with an elaborate arched torana as backdrop.  The scenes in the border register illustrate forms of torment to which mortals may be subjected, as listed in the Saddharmapundarika-sutra, a Mahayanist text mich revered in Nepal.  these scenes may be taken to represent the evils against which Amoghapasa is invoked.

physicalDescription: Shrine, of gilt silver, brass, and copper, repoussé and chased, enriched with filigree work and about 6000 precious stones, including diamonds, emeralds, rubies, sapphires, pearls, jacinths (zircons), lapis-lazuli, white and yellow topazes, as well as shaped pieces of turquoise, coral and white shell. On the facade of the shrine are five rectangular niches, three above and two below; the three above contain three seated figures representing respectively the Church (Sangha), the Buddha and the Law (Dharma) of Buddhism. The two standing figures in the lower two niches and the figure seated on the back of a Garuda in the middle of the surmounting pediment are all forms of the Patron Bodhisattva of the Lamaic Buddhists, Avalokitesvara. Each of the five panels has a broad frame round it, displaying the Eight Glorious Emblems of Buddhism, interspaced with bosses set with the mystic nine-gem (nau-ratan). Below is a wide lotus base set with coral and turquoise. At the two sides are two six-sides dragons, and two Makara-heads and nau-ratan bosses, all in gems and stones. Surmounting the pediment is a detachable three-tiered umbrella (chatra) of gilt copper and at the sides of the columns are two double flags of Nepal of gilt brass each with two applied plaques of silver repousse with the sacred syllable 'OM'. At each corner of the pediment hangs a flat tassel-like pendant with little leaves hanging from its points, and across the front from the tops of the columns is a silver chain hung with 37 jewelled drops. The foundation of the shrine is wood.

physicalDescription: Scroll painting (bilampau) depicting the life of the Buddha in four parts, on paper backed with cloth. The episodes correspond to the life of the Buddha as narrated in the Lalitavistara Sutra and include characteristically Nepali features, such as the initial visual invocation of Ganesha. The costumes and architecture locate the events in mid nineteenth century Nepal. For example, one scene shows the Buddha seated giving a discourse to an assembly in front of a depiction of the Swayambhu Caitya, with the white peaks of the Himalayas in the background. Annotations made in pencil give numbers running across the scroll painting, corresponding to a scene-by-scene description of the imagery recorded in the registers of the Asia Department at the V&A.

physicalDescription: Bronze crowned Buddha, likely identified as Akshobhya, seated in the 'earth touching' (bhūmisparśa mudrā) posture on a lotus pedestal. He wears a detachable crown, earrings and breast plate richly jewelled with turquoise, rubies, coral and other stones. The figure sits on an elaborate altar with detachable side pieces, an overarching back piece (prabhā-maṇḍala) displaying the five Buddhas (left to right): Akshobya, Ratnasambhava, Vairocana, Amitabha, and Amoghasiddhi. Kinnaras stand below these figures on either side, below which two Buddhas stand in a posture identified with the Buddha Dipankara. The lotus pedestal sits on a rectangular base supported by two elephants, who are associated with the Buddha Akshobhya, and lions. Several separate pieces show yalis standing on the backs on elephants. Two brass pillars terminate in figures of Garuda kneeling in a posture of devotion.

objectHistory:
This scarf was a collaboration between Citta and Tonic in 2009.
Tonic was a news and information website that published stories, features and profiles about good news and good deeds. Citta is a USA based non-profit organization working in India and Nepal to bring health, education and economic development of women to impoverished regions.

Celebrities were asked to give an inspiring word that meant something to them. These were then translated into Sanskrit, and encorporated into a scarf design by Lucy Barnes. The scarves were handknitted by the Citta Himilaya Women's Centre in Nepal. 

David Bowie contributed the word 'Funk'.  Thandie Newton 'Surrender' , Scarlett Johansson 'Reuse', David Byrne 'Dust' , Susan Sarandon 'Awake', Queen Latifah 'Strength', Sting 'Resolve', and Natalie Merchant 'Silent'.

The scarves were available in two colours; grey and camel. The proceeds from the scarf sales went towards Citta's charitable work.
briefDescription: Scarf made by Citta /Tonic and designed by Lucy Barnes, in colour 'Camel', 2009

physicalDescription: Figure of the Dharmapala Yama (the god of death) in his form of Phyi-sgrub (Chi-dup), of cast copper; the has a bull's head, red flaming hair and a crown of skulls; he has a third eye, a garland of skulls and the wheel ornament at his breast; he holds a skeleton-topped sceptre in his left hand (the pasa which he probably had in his right hand is missing) and steps to the right on a bull; the hair shows traces of red pigment, the face traces of blue and gold; a slot in the bull's back evidently held a figure of Yami (the god's sister) which is now missing; also the, apparently, bad fit of the bull's hoofs into their slots in the base suggests that, originally, the conventional figure of a woman was placed under the bull; an aureole of flames is located at the back. A rectangular opening at the back of the figure contains two mantras (IS.17A, B-1966), written on paper and wrapped in yellow silk.

objectHistory:
This was part of a collection of Indian, Nepalese, and Tibetan art objects that was purchased in 1913 from Imre Leonard Schwaiger was a well-respected London and Delhi-based dealer in gems, jewellery and eastern works of art. He was of Hungarian descent and, as a young man, he travelled to India where he became expert in appraising them, later becoming the foremost dealer and agent in such objects.
He built up a list of important clients and was friends with Jacques Cartier, looking after Cartier's interests in Delhi and acting as the company's agent in the purchase of gems, jewellery and objets d'art. Schwaiger was also responsible for introducing Cartier to all of the maharajas and other royals during his visit to India for the Dehi Durbar in 1911.
Imre Schwaiger developed a close working relationship with both the Victoria & Albert Museum and the British Museum, assisting them with a number of acquisitions. He also generously donated a number of valuable objects to both institutions.

Purchased from the dealer Imre Schwaiger, Esq., 39, Brook Street, Grosvenor Square, W. This acquisition information reflects that found in the Museum records (Asia Department registers and/or Central Inventory) as part of a 2023 provenance research project.

A heavily cast metal huqqa base, spherical, with a broad central frieze of vertical, rounded grooving. The bottom is undecorated; at the top is a moulded collar of overlapping lotus leaves, their tips curling upwards. The neck is low and circular. The opening for the huqqa 'snake' is embellished with an applied, almond-shaped plaque which has a raised, circular banded opening.

The composition of the metal is not easy to determine - it appears to have a greyish tinge underneath its brown patination, which may indicate a zinc alloy.
